text:
Omar El-Sayed: Kicking off design review coordination for KV compaction approach. I dropped a v0 outline here: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RT/KV+cache+compaction+design+v0

Main things I want eyes on before we lock the data structures:
1) pointer stability / how kernels find KV blocks after moves
2) stream sync constraints (prefill + decode overlap)
3) worst-case overhead (copy + metadata churn) + how we budget it

If folks can reply w/ concerns / “must not break” invariants, I’ll fold into the v1 doc.

Samir Qureshi: :eyes: read through. For #1, do we agree we can’t expose “raw device ptr” anywhere outside allocator internals? Today some kernels assume `base_ptr + block_id*stride` (fast). If blocks move, that breaks unless we add an indirection layer.

Hiro Tanaka: yeah, kernel side currently assumes contiguous-ish addressing. Not strictly contiguous across seqs, but the block_id -> ptr calc is arithmetic, not a load. If we add an indirection table lookup, that’s a perf hit on decode hot path.

Grace Kim: +1. Also correctness: compaction moving blocks while a decode kernel is in-flight is a non-starter. Even if we “update pointers”, the kernel already launched with the old address.

Noah Patel: I think we should separate “addressing model” vs “movement mechanism”. We can keep a stable *handle* per sequence (or per page) and implement movement by updating a page table that kernels consult *only when they build the gather list*.

But: we need to be clear where that gather list is built (CPU vs GPU) and how often.

Omar El-Sayed: current draft: per-request “block map” stored on host, mirrored to device (small int array) and passed to kernels. Kernel uses that to compute actual address. That’s an extra global load per block step.

Hiro Tanaka: can we avoid per-token global loads? Ideally we do one indirection per layer head chunk, not per token. But attention kernel reads K/V for every step, so it’s on the path.

Yuki Sato: in practice, how many “blocks per seq” are we touching per decode step? It’s basically all prior tokens => many blocks. So indirection table cache behavior matters.

Grace Kim: also: if indirection table itself is mutated by compaction, that’s another race. Need explicit lifetime rules: compactor can only mutate mapping when no kernel is reading that mapping.

Samir Qureshi: proposal: treat mapping as versioned. Each active request has `mapping_epoch`. Compaction creates a new mapping (or applies a patch list) and we only switch epoch when request reaches a safe point (between kernel launches).

Noah Patel: that’s basically RCU for the mapping. Might be too heavy but conceptually clean.

Marcus Reed: from perf suite POV, we can measure overhead separately:
- baseline decode with no compaction but with indirection lookup enabled
- compaction enabled w/ moves disabled (just eviction)
- compaction enabled full
That’ll tell us what’s “tax” vs “move cost”.

Benji Okafor: fwiw from flags/config, we can ship a mode matrix:
`kv_cache.addressing = arithmetic|indirect`
`kv_cache.compaction = off|evict_only|move`
Then we can canary addressing change first if needed.

Omar El-Sayed: 👍 that helps rollout.

Sofia Ivanova: question on #3 (worst-case overhead). What’s the budget model? If compaction fires under burst, we could steal time from decode and make tails worse.

Omar El-Sayed: draft budget: “bytes moved per second per GPU” cap + “max compaction ops per scheduling tick”. Triggered only when fragmentation_ratio > X and allocator pressure high. But I’m not confident on how to translate to latency impact.

Hiro Tanaka: budget in terms of *GPU time* is what matters. Bytes moved is proxy but depends on path (device-to-device copy, alignment, stream sync). If we do any sync w/ default stream it’s game over.

Grace Kim: exactly. Stream semantics:
- decode kernels run on stream D
- prefill on stream P (sometimes same stream depending on model family)
Compactor needs its own stream C and must use events to avoid moving blocks that are “in use” by D/P.

At minimum: record an event after the last kernel that might touch a victim block, then make C wait on that event before copying.

Grace Kim: pseudo:
```
// on decode stream
cudaEventRecord(kv_safe_event, decode_stream);

// on compaction stream
cudaStreamWaitEvent(compact_stream, kv_safe_event);
memcpy_async(compact_stream, dst, src, bytes);
cudaEventRecord(compact_done_event, compact_stream);

// before next decode that uses moved block
cudaStreamWaitEvent(decode_stream, compact_done_event);
```
But if we do this per-block we’ll drown in events.

Samir Qureshi: event storm is my concern too. Could batch compaction into “windows”: only compact blocks whose owning sequences are currently idle / not scheduled for decode this tick.

Sofia Ivanova: scheduler can help: we know which requests are in active decode set vs queued. We can expose a “do-not-touch” set to compactor (all active this tick + any with pending prefill).

Noah Patel: careful: queued doesn’t mean safe. We can have in-flight kernels for a request even if it’s not in the scheduler’s current runnable list (e.g., overlap from prior tick). Need explicit “in_flight” accounting from runtime.

Yuki Sato: we already track `request->cuda_fence` for stream sync in a couple places. Can we reuse that? Like each request has a last-used event, compactor only touches blocks for requests whose event is completed.

Grace Kim: yes, per-request fence is the right primitive. Then compactor uses `cudaEventQuery` (or a cheap polling wrapper) to pick eligible victims without synchronizing.

Hiro Tanaka: if we use event query, make sure we don’t call into CUDA driver too often on CPU and burn cycles. Might need a sampling/backoff.

Marcus Reed: can we define acceptance: “compaction bookkeeping CPU < 1% core” or something? We should measure on burst benchmarks.

Omar El-Sayed: 👍 Adding to doc: “CPU overhead ceiling” and “CUDA API call rate” metrics.

Samir Qureshi: back to pointer stability: what if we keep arithmetic addressing for the majority by moving only within a fixed-size slab? i.e., blocks are movable but within same slab base pointer, so `base + idx*stride` still holds if we update idx? That still requires idx indirection somewhere.

Hiro Tanaka: updating idx implies you store idx per sequence per block, which is the mapping table again. Arithmetic addressing only works if block IDs are stable and physical layout is stable.

Noah Patel: alternative: “segment compaction” where we compact whole segments (large contiguous ranges) and keep per-seq segments mostly fixed. Then mapping is per-segment, not per-block. Less indirection, fewer updates.

Omar El-Sayed: that’s in the working notes as “2-tier: hot segments (pinned) + cold segments (movable)”. But it complicates eviction: hot pinned means holes accumulate there.

Sofia Ivanova: from scheduler POV, hot/cold fits: active decode sequences = hot, idle/prefix-cached = cold. We can bias compaction to cold; eviction policy already will hit cold first. That might reduce how often we ever need to move hot.

Grace Kim: I’m ok with “move cold only” as a safety constraint for v1. Then pointer stability issue is limited to cold pages. But cold pages are still used when a request resumes / cache hit, so mapping needs to be correct.

Yuki Sato: if cold pages aren’t touched frequently, indirection penalty might be acceptable there (not on every decode step). That’s appealing.

Hiro Tanaka: +1 if we can keep hot path unchanged. We can implement compaction on cold side first, prove it helps fragmentation, then iterate.

Omar El-Sayed: sounds like consensus forming:
- v1: compaction moves only cold / non-running requests
- keep decode kernel arithmetic addressing for hot pages
- introduce indirection only for cold pages OR at request resume boundary

Question: how do we handle a request transitioning cold->hot? Do we “re-materialize” into hot slab? That’s a copy anyway.

Noah Patel: that’s basically a promotion. We can do promotion lazily on first decode after resume: allocate hot blocks, copy from cold, update request metadata. Similar to paging.

Grace Kim: promotion needs same stream safety rules. But it’s per-request, easier to fence than global compaction.

Benji Okafor: rollout wise, we can guard promotion w/ flag too. Something like:
- enable cold compaction + no promotion (only affects prefix cache store?)
- then enable promotion when stable

Marcus Reed: perf tests we’ll need:
- prefix-cache heavy workload (resume rate high)
- mixed prefill/decode under burst
- worst-case long context + lots of short completions (fragmentation creator)
I can add a microbench for “resume storm”.

Redwood Review Bot: Reminder: design review scheduled for Wed 11:00 PT. Please add agenda items to the doc 2 hours prior. (reacted :spiral_calendar_pad:)

Omar El-Sayed: thx all. Action items I’m taking:
- update design w/ “cold-only compaction” constraint + promotion path sketch
- define invariants: no moving pages for requests w/ incomplete CUDA fence; no per-block events
- add explicit overhead metrics: mapping lookup tax, CUDA API call rate, bytes moved, GPU time

If anyone has strong objections to cold/hot split, drop them here before EOD.

Hiro Tanaka: no objection. Only ask: document precisely what is “hot” in terms of kernel access (decode tick? prefill? speculative decode?). We’ve got a couple execution modes.

Grace Kim: +1. Also please call out “default stream forbidden” in compaction code path. We’ve been burned before.

Omar El-Sayed: noted. Will add a big ⚠️ section in the doc (no default stream, no device-wide sync). (reacted :thumbsup:)

Sofia Ivanova: I’ll write up what scheduler can provide as signals:
- active_request_set
- cache_pressure scalar
- per-tenant priority class
and what we *can’t* reliably provide (kernel in-flight).

Omar El-Sayed: perfect. I’ll ping you for a snippet to include.

Samir Qureshi: quick last note: we should decide whether mapping table lives in unified memory vs explicit device buffer. UM could simplify but unpredictable page faults.

Yuki Sato: avoid UM for this. We had UM page migrations show up as random p99 spikes in profiling last year.

Omar El-Sayed: agreed, explicit device buffer for mapping. Will capture in ADR notes.
